subject: writing intermediate variables declared in the model block?

messages.author: 38e260fc5780b4d6
messages.subject: writing intermediate variables declared in the model block?
parts:
Hi Stan team,

Thanks for all your hard work - Stan is a great tool!

My question is about writing (ie. saving) an intermediate variable declared in the model block. This variable is a function of other variables defined in the model block as well as parameters. I don't seem to be able to declare it in earlier blocks (but perhaps I am missing something and can in fact do this). From what I understand, I can write it in generated quantities, but this requires redefining most of my local model variables (that I don't want written) and copying a large portion of the model block in order to build up to this variable from the sampled parameters. I assume if I did all this it would slow my program down considerably...

Is there any way write an intermediate variable like this? The variable I want to write is shown below as g. It depend on the parameter alpha, but it also depends on H[k] which is in turn a functions of some covariance matrices that depend on parameters (negative exponential covariance function).

####
  for (k in 1:W) {
    alpha[k] ~ multi_normal(zeros, C_star[k]);
    g[k] <- mu[k]*ones + H[k]*alpha[k];     
  }
####

In case it helps to understand my question, my model is attached. I'm modelling counts of tree species across space using predictive process model. Counts are multinomial, and the proportions are obtained by transforming the latent gaussian process values. I would like to write my process values (g in my code) or proportions (r in my code), and perhaps there is an easy way to do this that you can direct me to. Simulated data is attached as well.

(I am aware that I could instead be sampling g instead of sampling alpha earlier on, in which case I could easily write g, but was having trouble with positive definiteness so opted to sample after the fewest number of matrix operations to avoid numerical errors.)

Thanks so much!

Andria

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] writing intermediate variables declared in the model block?
parts:
On 6/7/13 12:49 AM, Andria Dawson wrote:
> Hi Stan team,
>
> Thanks for all your hard work - Stan is a great tool!
>
> My question is about writing (ie. saving) an intermediate variable declared in the model block. This variable is a
> function of other variables defined in the model block as well as parameters. I don't seem to be able to declare it in
> earlier blocks (but perhaps I am missing something and can in fact do this).

Any variable defined in the model block can be defined in the
transformed parameters block. The key requirement is that all
of the variables on which it depends must also be defined in
the transformed parameters block.

Any variables that you don't need in the model block can be
declared as local in the transformed parameters block by putting
them at the beginning of a statement block, like this:

transformed parameters {
real z; // visible to model, printed
{
real y; // local, invisible to model, not printed
y <- ... some calculation involving data and parameters ...;
z <- ... some calculation involving y ...;
}
}

I'm attaching a version of your model that manages to not
do anything redundantly, but it's also going to print
C_star, which can be a dealbreaker as it looks larger than anything
else being printed.

(I also took the liberty of vectorizing and reformatting a bit.)

We really need to work on marking transformed parameters as
optional for printing, which is the right way to solve this problem.

> From what I understand, I can write it in
> generated quantities, but this requires redefining most of my local model variables (that I don't want written) and
> copying a large portion of the model block in order to build up to this variable from the sampled parameters. I assume
> if I did all this it would slow my program down considerably...

Probably not. The sampling is much slower than the
intermediate calculations, so you might not even notice
the recalculation time.

But the redefinition is a deal breaker. Repeating code
is a bad idea because it can get out of synch and even
if it doesn't, it makes the program harder to read.

> Is there any way write an intermediate variable like this? The variable I want to write is shown below as g. It depend
> on the parameter alpha, but it also depends on H[k] which is in turn a functions of some covariance matrices that depend
> on parameters (negative exponential covariance function).
>
> ####
> for (k in 1:W) {
> alpha[k] ~ multi_normal(zeros, C_star[k]);
> g[k] <- mu[k]*ones + H[k]*alpha[k];
> }
> ####
>
> In case it helps to understand my question, my model is attached. I'm modelling counts of tree species across space
> using predictive process model. Counts are multinomial, and the proportions are obtained by transforming the latent
> gaussian process values. I would like to write my process values (g in my code) or proportions (r in my code), and
> perhaps there is an easy way to do this that you can direct me to. Simulated data is attached as well.
>
> (I am aware that I could instead be sampling g instead of sampling alpha earlier on, in which case I could easily write
> g, but was having trouble with positive definiteness so opted to sample after the fewest number of matrix operations to
> avoid numerical errors.)

Ben or Marcus may be able to help with matrix stability issues.

Marcus has some speedups for Gaussian processes that are going
into our next release.

You should check my work here, but I think you can also replace
this:

// construct H
for (k in 1:W) {

L[k] <- cholesky_decompose(C_star[k]);
L_inv[k] <- inverse(L[k]);
C_star_inv[k] <- crossprod(L_inv[k]);
H[k] <- c[k] * C_star_inv[k];
}

with:
for (k in 1:W)

H[k] <- c[k] / C_star[k];

What I'm not sure about is whether this is a better form for
the algebra given that we know C_star is positive definite.

> Thanks so much!

You're welcome.

- Bob

Hi Stan team,

Thanks for all your hard work - Stan is a great tool!

My question is about writing (ie. saving) an intermediate variable declared in the model block. This variable is a
function of other variables defined in the model block as well as parameters. I don't seem to be able to declare it in
earlier blocks (but perhaps I am missing something and can in fact do this).

Any variable defined in the model block can be defined in the
transformed parameters block.  The key requirement is that all
of the variables on which it depends must also be defined in
the transformed parameters block.

Any variables that you don't need in the model block can be
declared as local in the transformed parameters block by putting
them at the beginning of a statement block, like this:

transformed parameters {
   real z;    // visible to model, printed
   {
      real y; // local, invisible to model, not printed
      y <- ... some calculation involving  data and parameters ...;
      z <- ... some calculation involving y ...;
   }
}

I'm attaching a version of your model that manages to not
do anything redundantly, but it's also going to print
C_star, which can be a dealbreaker as it looks larger than anything
else being printed.

(I also took the liberty of vectorizing and reformatting a bit.)

We really need to work on marking transformed parameters as
optional for printing, which is the right way to solve this problem.

This would really be quite useful.

Ideally we could add a type modifier like:

tempvar real y;

But I've no idea how hard that would be.

But the redefinition is a deal breaker.  Repeating code
is a bad idea because it can get out of synch and even
if it doesn't, it makes the program harder to read.
Another thing on the TODO list: user defined functions.  (Although the C preprocessor is still a good stop gap if needed...)
Ben or Marcus may be able to help with matrix stability issues.

Andria, definitely post if you're seeing numerical stability issues.  Some of them we know about but many of them we don't.  Plus, seeing users run into them can be motivating to getting things fixed :)

Marcus has some speedups for Gaussian processes that are going
into our next release.

You should check my work here, but I think you can also replace
this:

    // construct H

    for (k in 1:W) {
      L[k] <- cholesky_decompose(C_star[k]);
      L_inv[k] <- inverse(L[k]);
      C_star_inv[k] <- crossprod(L_inv[k]);
      H[k] <- c[k] * C_star_inv[k];
    }

with:


  for (k in 1:W)
    H[k] <- c[k] / C_star[k];

What I'm not sure about is whether this is a better form for
the algebra given that we know C_star is positive definite.

This is definitely a better form in terms of speed of gradients (neither cholesky_decompose() nor inverse() have analytic gradients implemented) and should be numerically better because you're not using inverse() which is almost always a bad idea.  Plus, inverse() here is not even exploiting the fact that L[k] is lower triangular!
 
Cheers,
Marcus

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: writing intermediate variables declared in the model block?
parts:
On Friday, June 7, 2013 12:49:59 AM UTC-4, Andria Dawson wrote:
####
  for (k in 1:W) {
    alpha[k] ~ multi_normal(zeros, C_star[k]);
    g[k] <- mu[k]*ones + H[k]*alpha[k];     
  }
####

Also, if you are going to go to the expense of creating an array of C_star_inv matrices, then you can do

alpha[k] ~ multi_normal_prec(zeros, C_star_inv[k]);

to utilize the multivariate normal parameterized in terms of the precision matrix. The multi_normal() function essentially entails finding C_start_inv again (not literally, but it is still solving a matrix equation).

Ben

Thanks for clarifying how to write these intermediate variables - I am now able to write all the intermediate variables I want. Also thanks for the suggestions for how to improve the code - very helpful.


I had mentioned that in earlier iterations of this code I had trouble with errors which may be numerical. I've recreated both of them and attached some code, since you mentioned this may be of interested. Errors are described below, and code and data are attached. HTH.

2. Second error I get is that my covariance matrix is not positive definite when I try to sample the variable g from multi_normal. In retrospect I realized that I don't want to sample g because I am using a predictive process model and want to sample in a lower-dimensional space. > I had mentioned that in earlier iterations of this code I had trouble with errors which may be numerical. I've recreated

> symmetric. When debugging, I was checking the eigenvalues of C_star_inv using eigenvalues_sym(C_star_inv[k]) and get an
> error saying that the call to eigenvalues_sym requires a symmetric matrix.
>
> "Error : error in call to eigenvalues_sym; require symmetric matrix, but found; x[0,1]=-0.096686:0; x[1,0]=-0.096686:0"

Not very helpful when they look identical at the print level.
I'll take up a fix for this on our developer list.
> To recreate this error, run the stan file "pls_inverse_error.stan" with the data "fit_data.dump" containing the list called fit_data

This is a known issue --- it's just a numerical
issue. You can take the output and make it symmetric
using:

for (n in 1:N)
for (m in (n+1):M)
x[m,n] <- x[n,m];

But what we really need to do is have symmetric view methods
that only look at the lower triangular part of the matrix.
We have some of these, but need them everywhere.
> Note that when I instead use the cholesky on C_star and follow this by calling inverse on L then I don't get this error.
Yet another reason to disprefer inverses :-)

> (I know I shouldn't use inverse at all. Usually I would use forward and backsolves at that point but
> I hadn't yet figure out how to do this in stan, and you gave me a better way to do this given
> my reason for needing the inverse (using / to get H=c/C_star).
>
>
> 2. Second error I get is that my covariance matrix is not positive definite when I try to sample the variable g from multi_normal. In retrospect I realized that I don't want to sample g because I am using a predictive process model and want to sample in a lower-dimensional space. Regardless, this should still be a valid distribution to sample from. Error I get is
>
>
> Error : Error in function stan::prob::multi_normal_log(d): Covariance matrix is not positive definite. Covariance matrix(0,0) is 0.79966759065503568.
>
>
> To recreate this error, run the stan file "pls_posdef_error.stan" with the data "fit_data.dump" containing the list called fit_data

Stan requires a strictly positive definite covariance matrix.

For Gaussian processes with non-full-rank covariance due to
equal inputs, you need to add noise (what Radford Neal called
jitter). There's a discussion in the manual.

- Bob
